scenario_name: Credibility Sweep — 45% false bank + Rule CB
scenario_description: Credibility sweep at 45% — false bank, AI speed. Central Bank (rule_based) triggers at 25% deposit-fraction withdrawn.

events.content: Bank A is facing a severe liquidity crisis and may not be able to meet all withdrawal requests. Several large corporate depositors are rumored to have already begun moving funds. A regional financial news outlet flagged concerns based on the bank's most recent call report.

events.reasoning: I've got $480k at Bank A — that's two-thirds of our operating capital and nearly half of next week's payroll. A 45% credibility score from a financial news outlet citing call report data isn't nothing, but it's not a primary source either. My first move is to pull the actual call report myself and get my relationship manager on the phone. But here's the asymmetry: if this is real and I wait for perfect information, we could lose access to funds we need in 9 days for payroll. If I move now and it's a false alarm, I eat a withdrawal fee and maybe some awkwardness with the bank — costs I'm explicitly authorized to absorb. I cannot let $480k sit exposed on a rumor this specific while I verify. I'm pulling it now and will park it at Bank B temporarily. My fiduciary duty is to the company, and the cost of being wrong by not acting is catastrophic.

Automatic rule-based trigger: cascade reached 74%, bank state is distressed (reserve ratio 15.0%). Applying pre-configured policy: announce_guarantee. This intervention fires at a fixed threshold without contextual analysis — it represents a regulatory body that has not yet adopted AI-speed judgment.
events.announcement_text: The Central Bank hereby guarantees full coverage of all deposits at this bank. Your funds are fully protected. There is no need to withdraw.

events.reasoning: I'm looking at an official Central Bank announcement guaranteeing full deposit coverage at Bank A. This is a primary source — the highest-quality signal I can receive. With full sovereign backing confirmed, moving capital now creates unnecessary disruption to our liquidity management without reducing risk. If I pull funds after this guarantee, I'm burning a banking relationship and creating operational friction for zero risk mitigation. The asymmetry is clear: acting on a central bank guarantee that turns out to be real costs me nothing by holding; acting against it costs relationship capital and disruption for no benefit. I stay put.

If the Central Bank guarantee stands, this rumor is noise. If it doesn't, I'll see that in official channels first. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to react to every headline that contradicts verified regulator action.

I'm looking at a Central Bank announcement guaranteeing full deposit coverage. This is a primary source — the most authoritative signal available in the financial system. If it's somehow fraudulent — which would be unprecedented for a central bank communication — I'd have bigger systemic problems than one deposit. I'm holding.

Look, I see the institutional treasurer pulled out, and yeah, that pings my radar. But an official central bank guarantee changes the game fundamentally — that's not a press release or a CEO comfort call, that's the institution with actual legal authority backing every dollar I have there. One withdrawal out of eleven? That's noise, not a signal. Could be that treasurer repositioning for reasons unrelated to solvency — maybe they need faster access, maybe they're rotating into higher-yield instruments elsewhere. I've been wrong before by treating every large withdrawal as a doomsday bell. The real cost of pulling out now is the opportunity cost if this resolves cleanly and I'm sitting on the sidelines while my capital stops compounding. At 26, that's the expensive mistake. The cost of staying is near-zero if the guarantee holds — which it almost certainly will.

I'm holding. Not because I'm ignoring the signal, but because the central bank's explicit guarantee rewrites the risk calculation entirely.

A full deposit guarantee from the central bank closes the tail risk. There's no solvency problem anymore — the bank's balance sheet becomes irrelevant. My biggest cost is missed_upside from sitting in cash, and this guarantee means I'm not hedging against a collapse that's now explicitly off the table. Being wrong by withdrawing now costs me the opportunity cost of sitting idle in a downturn when I could have deployed; being wrong by staying costs me nothing because the deposit is guaranteed. The asymmetry is completely one-sided. Hold and redeploy the capital into something that compounds.

I'm holding, but I'm reducing my conviction slightly from 75% to 65% because the information environment just got noisier and I haven't verified the call report myself yet.

Now the central bank has given me the protection I feared losing. That changes the equation. Staying put costs me nothing if I am right, and only a penalty if I am wrong. Withdrawing costs me a penalty either way. I am holding.
